summary: Ara Khan opens by stating most people are wrong about evals, identifying two camps: the objective metrics camp treating leaderboard numbers as definitive, and the taste camp relying on vibes. The truth is inconveniently in between. He proposes three stages of eval maturity and three heuristics: never trust model-lab eval numbers, avoid being the earliest adopter, and seek new precise evals because standardized benchmarks like HumanEval no longer measure frontier coding. He frames evals as both engineering and philosophy, where the core difficulty is approximating an infinite failure search space. Cline initially dismissed standardized evals, then built custom evals from opt-in user data before adopting Stanford's Terminal Bench with 89 real-world coding problems. Terminal Bench works by giving each task an isolated VM environment with the repo and setup, installing any coding agent CLI, and running all tasks in parallel using Harbor infrastructure software from Loda Institute. The limiting factor becomes the slowest task, with some taking 30-40 minutes. After a run yielding a score, you portfolio-allocate failures by sending another agent through all failure traces to identify small levers that move the score. Testing actually evaluates three things: the model itself, the harness (whether it leverages the model well), and whether the problems are worth solving. Cline's original Terminal Bench score was 43%. Improvements came from container CPU/memory settings, raised timeouts, and thinking behavior tuning—not from switching models. Khan warns that asking models to think more can backfire when models loop. He identifies three zones of improvement after each run: zone one is obvious bugs like crashes or rate limits; zone two is nuance improvements like model-family-specific prompt engineering techniques that work for Anthropic but not Codex or Gemini; zone three is overfitting to the benchmark, which he explicitly warns against. The final guidance is to hill-climb on a benchmark—improving your harness score while also passing the vibe check of whether the product feels good to use. Cline discovered through hill-climbing that supporting Gemini and Kimi model families, where they were initially weaker, would unlock new user segments.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Two Camps of Eval Error
sections.summary: Khan introduces the talk title and critiques how people use evals. He identifies two camps of wrongness: the objective metrics camp that treats benchmark numbers as definitive, and the taste camp that relies on vibes. The truth is in the middle—evals are neither end-all-be-all nor useless.

sections.title: Three Stages and Three Heuristics for Evals
sections.summary: Khan outlines three stages of eval usage and three heuristics: don't trust model-lab numbers, don't be the earliest adopter, and seek new precise evals. He cites OpenAI's blog acknowledging HumanEval no longer measures frontier coding and notes the rapid frontier model turnover per Epochs Index.

sections.title: Evals as Engineering and Philosophy Problem
sections.summary: Khan frames evals as both engineering and philosophy problems. The core philosophical challenge is approximating the infinite search space of where problems can fail, even in coding. He introduces Cline as an open-source coding company and describes their early dismissal of standardized evals.

sections.title: Cline's Eval Building Journey and Terminal Bench
sections.summary: Khan describes Cline's process of building custom evals from opt-in user data, paying users, and manually cleaning problems. He contrasts single-turn LLM evals with difficult multi-step agentic evals where agents read files, search docs, install environments, and run tests. He introduces Stanford's Terminal Bench with 89 real-world coding problems.

sections.title: Running Terminal Bench and Portfolio Allocation of Failures
sections.summary: Khan explains Terminal Bench mechanics: each task gets an isolated VM with repo and setup, any coding agent CLI is installed, and Harbor software from Loda Institute runs all 89 tasks in parallel. After getting a score, you portfolio-allocate failures by running another agent through failure traces to identify small levers. He notes evals test three things: the model, the harness, and whether problems are worth solving.

sections.title: Three Zones of Improvement and Hill Climbing
sections.summary: Khan describes Cline's 43% starting score and improvements from CPU/memory, timeouts, and thinking behavior. He introduces three zones: zone one is obvious bugs, zone two is nuance improvements like model-family-specific prompt engineering, zone three is overfitting to avoid. He concludes by urging listeners to hill-climb on a benchmark while also passing the vibe check, and shares that Cline discovered supporting more model families unlocked new user segments.
